timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: I SSH into my server all the time. Just type the password and I'm in, right?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Peter, you should never use password authentication for SSH. Use key-based authentication. Passwords can be brute-forced, but SSH keys are practically unbreakable.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: You generate a key pair - a public key and a private key. The public key goes on the server, the private key stays on your machine. Authentication happens through cryptographic proof, not passwords.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Critical configuration: disable root login, change the default port, use fail2ban to block brute-force attempts, and use Ed25519 keys instead of RSA.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Ed25519 keys are shorter (256 bits vs 2048+) but more secure. They're also faster and resistant to side-channel attacks. RSA is legacy at this point.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: SSH tunneling is incredibly powerful. You can forward ports, create VPNs, and bypass firewalls - all through SSH. But that means attackers can use it for lateral movement.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: So if I have SSH access, I can move through the whole network?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: If SSH keys are shared or poorly managed, absolutely. That's why zero-trust networks require authentication for every connection, not just the perimeter.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Interview tip: explain SSH key-based authentication, list hardening steps, and describe how SSH tunneling works. You'll be tested on this.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: I'm switching to key-based auth right now.
